# 1. Application context

Governments want to direct social transfers to the poorest households. In Latin America
many workers are informal, so income is hard to verify. Countries therefore use *proxy
means tests*: they predict poverty from observable household characteristics (dwelling,
assets, household composition, education) instead of income (Caruso, Galiani and
Weinschelbaum, 2019).

**Data.** Household survey from Costa Rica (Inter-American Development Bank, released on
Kaggle: "Costa Rican Household Poverty Level Prediction"). The original data has one row per
person (9,557 persons in 2,988 households). Because the poverty label belongs to the
household, we keep **one row per household (the household head)**. Otherwise members of the
same household could end up in both the training and the test data. After cleaning we have
**`r format(nrow(costa_rica), big.mark = ",")` households and `r ncol(costa_rica) - 1`
predictors**.

**Task.** Classification: is a household *poor* (extreme or moderate poverty) or *not poor*
(vulnerable or non-vulnerable)? This mirrors the decision of a targeting programme: is the
household eligible or not? The label `poor` is known for every household in the survey. We
use it to train the models and to check them on households that the models have not seen.

**Why the type of error matters.** Classifying a poor household as not poor excludes it from
support. Classifying a non-poor household as poor wastes resources. Which error is worse is a
policy choice, so besides the error rate we use sensitivity, specificity and the AUC.

**Related work.** Kim (2021) fits a random forest and gradient boosted trees to the original
four-class problem on the same data and also finds education to be the most important
predictor. Our set-up differs (binary target, one row per household).

# 2. The data: variables and meaning

`head_` refers to the household head, `n_` means "number of". In the exploratory analysis
categorical variables are factors (one variable instead of many 0/1 columns).

| Group | Variables | Meaning | Why we expect it to matter |
|---|---|---|---|
| Household head | `head_age`, `head_male`, `head_marital_status`, `head_education_level`, `head_years_schooling`, `head_disabled` | Characteristics of the head | Education is the classic driver of earnings; female-headed households are often poorer |
| Composition | `household_size`, `persons_living_in_dwelling`, `n_children_0_19`, `n_seniors_65plus`, `n_males_under12`, `n_males_12plus`, `n_females_under12`, `n_females_12plus`, `dependency_rate`, `mean_years_schooling_adults` | Size and age structure; dependency rate = (members under 19 or over 64) / members aged 19-64; average schooling of adults | Many dependants per earner and low adult education mean low income per person |
| Dwelling | `n_rooms`, `n_bedrooms`, `persons_per_bedroom`, `overcrowded_bedrooms`, `overcrowded_rooms`, `housing_tenure`, `monthly_rent`, `wall_material`, `wall_quality`, `roof_material`, `roof_quality`, `has_ceiling`, `floor_material`, `floor_quality` | Size, crowding, tenure and building quality | Dwelling quality is the core of a proxy means test |
| Services | `water_supply`, `electricity_source`, `toilet_type`, `has_toilet`, `cooking_energy`, `rubbish_disposal` | Access to water, electricity, sanitation, cooking fuel, waste collection | Lack of basic services signals deprivation |
| Assets | `has_refrigerator`, `has_computer`, `has_television`, `n_tablets`, `n_mobile_phones` | Durable goods | Assets are a direct proxy of wealth |
| Location | `region`, `urban` | Planning region; urban (1) or rural (0) | Regional and rural-urban gaps in development |
| **Target** | `poor` | `poor` = original groups 1-2, `not_poor` = groups 3-4 | |

```{r overview}
predictors <- setdiff(names(costa_rica), "poor")
X <- costa_rica[predictors]

# type of each predictor: categorical (factor), binary (0/1) or numeric
var_type <- sapply(X, function(x) {
  if (is.factor(x)) "categorical"
  else if (all(x %in% c(0, 1))) "binary 0/1"
  else "numeric"
})
table(var_type)

# helper: to which original variable does a column of the model data belong?
# (e.g. "wall_material_wood" -> "wall_material"; numeric columns keep their name)
col_to_var <- function(cols) {
  sapply(cols, function(cn) {
    hits <- predictors[startsWith(cn, predictors)]
    hits[which.max(nchar(hits))]
  }, USE.NAMES = FALSE)
}

dim(costa_rica)          # readable version: households x (predictors + poor)
dim(costa_rica_model)    # model version:    households x (columns + poor)
sum(is.na(costa_rica)) + sum(is.na(costa_rica_model))   # missing values left
```

In the model version every category is its own 0/1 column named `<variable>_<category>`, for
example `wall_material_wood` = 1 if the walls are made of wood, 0 otherwise.

## Data cleaning (script `01_clean_data.R`)

| Step | Decision | Reason |
|---|---|---|
| Unit of observation | Kept only the household head (9,557 persons -> 2,973 households) | The poverty label is a household outcome. Several rows per household would put the same household in training and test data (leakage). |
| Households without a head | 15 of 2,988 households dropped (0.5%) | They have no head row to keep. |
| Target | Built `poor` from the head's 4-class group and removed the 4-class variable | A binary target is simpler and mirrors the eligibility decision. Keeping the 4-class variable would predict `poor` perfectly (leakage). In 85 households the members disagree on the group, so we use the head's. |
| Text values | "yes"/"no" in `dependency_rate` set to 1/0 | Checked against the squared columns of the original data. |
| Structural missing values | `monthly_rent` and `n_tablets` set to 0 when missing | They are missing exactly when the household pays no rent / owns no tablet, so 0 is the true value. |
| Other missing values | 3 households without adult schooling dropped; `rez_esc` (missing for all but one head) removed | Dropping 3 of 2,973 rows is negligible. `rez_esc` is only defined for school-age persons. |
| Redundant columns | Removed squared copies, exact sums of other columns, duplicates and constant columns | They add no information and only create collinearity. |
| Categories | Merged the 0/1 columns of one characteristic into one factor (for example `wall_material`) with readable labels; households in none of the listed categories get the label `not_recorded` | Easier to read. These are hidden missing values (for example `roof_material` 19 households). |
| Dummy variables | Model data: one 0/1 column for every category, no reference category | Every category gets its own coefficient, which is easy to interpret and compare. |
| Rare columns | 0/1 columns in which one value occurs in fewer than 30 households are removed | The effect of such a column cannot be estimated reliably (with 22% poor, 30 households contain only about 7 poor ones). No household is removed and the target is not used. |

**Result:** `r nrow(costa_rica)` households, `r ncol(costa_rica) - 1` predictors in the
readable data (`r sum(var_type == "categorical")` categorical, `r sum(var_type == "binary 0/1")`
binary, `r sum(var_type == "numeric")` numeric) and `r ncol(costa_rica_model) - 1` 0/1 or
numeric columns in the model data. No missing values, one row per household.

**What we can rely on:** each household appears once, the target is consistent with the
variables, the only recodings of values ("yes"/"no", structural zeros) were checked against
other columns, and no predictor contains information on the target (no leakage). Nothing was
removed because of its relation to poverty; variable selection is left to the models,
inside cross-validation.

**Limitations (kept on purpose):**

* The data describe the household head and the dwelling, not every member.
* The classes are imbalanced (22% poor).
* Some columns are strongly correlated (see section 6.2).
* Rent is skewed and the dependency rate is capped.

# 3. The target

```{r target}
table(costa_rica$poor)
round(100 * prop.table(table(costa_rica$poor)), 1)
ggplot(costa_rica, aes(poor, fill = poor)) + geom_bar() +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Households") + theme(legend.position = "none")
```

`r round(100 * mean(costa_rica$poor == "poor"))`% of the households are poor
(`r sum(costa_rica$poor == "poor")` of `r nrow(costa_rica)`). The rule "nobody is poor" is
already right for `r round(100 * mean(costa_rica$poor == "not_poor"))`% of the households, so
**accuracy alone is misleading**. We evaluate with sensitivity, specificity and AUC.

# 4. Who is poor? Descriptive analysis

```{r helper}
overall <- 100 * mean(costa_rica$poor == "poor")

# bar chart of the poverty rate for each group, with the number of households (n)
plot_rate <- function(group, title) {
  d <- data.frame(group = group, poor = costa_rica$poor == "poor")
  d <- d[!is.na(d$group), ]
  r <- aggregate(poor ~ group, d, function(x) c(rate = 100 * mean(x), n = length(x)))
  r <- data.frame(group = r$group, rate = r$poor[, "rate"], n = r$poor[, "n"])
  ggplot(r, aes(reorder(group, rate), rate)) + geom_col() +
    geom_text(aes(label = paste0("n=", n)), hjust = -0.1, size = 3) +
    geom_hline(yintercept = overall, linetype = "dashed") +
    coord_flip() + scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 100)) +
    labs(x = NULL, y = "Poverty rate (%)", title = title, subtitle = "dashed: overall rate")
}
```

**Education, region, area and sex of the head**

```{r groups}
# education of the head in 5 groups (the household with level "not_recorded" is left out)
edu_map <- c(none = "none / incomplete primary",
             incomplete_primary = "none / incomplete primary",
             complete_primary = "complete primary",
             incomplete_secondary = "incomplete secondary",
             incomplete_technical_secondary = "incomplete secondary",
             complete_secondary = "complete secondary",
             complete_technical_secondary = "complete secondary",
             undergraduate_or_higher = "higher",
             postgraduate = "higher")
edu_group <- unname(edu_map[as.character(costa_rica$head_education_level)])

plot_rate(edu_group, "By education of the head")
plot_rate(costa_rica$region, "By region")
plot_rate(ifelse(costa_rica$urban == 1, "urban", "rural"), "Urban vs rural")
plot_rate(ifelse(costa_rica$head_male == 1, "male head", "female head"), "By sex of the head")
```

**Assets and dwelling**

```{r assets}
# for each 0/1 indicator: poverty rate of households with (=1) and without (=0)
assets <- data.frame(
  has_computer         = costa_rica$has_computer,
  has_tablet           = as.numeric(costa_rica$n_tablets > 0),
  has_refrigerator     = costa_rica$has_refrigerator,
  has_television       = costa_rica$has_television,
  has_ceiling          = costa_rica$has_ceiling,
  overcrowded_bedrooms = costa_rica$overcrowded_bedrooms)
long <- do.call(rbind, lapply(names(assets), function(v)
  data.frame(var = v, has = ifelse(assets[[v]] == 1, "yes (=1)", "no (=0)"),
             poor = costa_rica$poor == "poor")))
res_assets <- aggregate(poor ~ var + has, long, function(x) 100 * mean(x))
ggplot(res_assets, aes(var, poor, fill = has)) + geom_col(position = "dodge") +
  coord_flip() + labs(x = NULL, y = "Poverty rate (%)", fill = NULL)

plot_rate(costa_rica$floor_quality, "By floor quality")
plot_rate(costa_rica$housing_tenure, "By type of tenure")
```

**Numeric variables**

```{r numeric}
num_vars <- c("head_years_schooling", "mean_years_schooling_adults",
              "persons_per_bedroom", "n_children_0_19",
              "household_size", "dependency_rate")
summary(costa_rica[num_vars])
long <- data.frame(poor  = rep(costa_rica$poor, length(num_vars)),
                   var   = rep(num_vars, each = nrow(costa_rica)),
                   value = unlist(costa_rica[num_vars], use.names = FALSE))
ggplot(long, aes(poor, value, fill = poor)) + geom_boxplot() +
  facet_wrap(~ var, scales = "free_y") + labs(x = NULL, y = NULL) +
  theme(legend.position = "none")
```

# 5. Which variables are most related to poverty?

We use the model data, in which every category is its own 0/1 column. Each category then
gets its own correlation with `poor` (1 = poor). A correlation has no units, so numeric
variables and categories can be compared directly. Positive = more often poor.

```{r correlations}
Xd <- as.matrix(costa_rica_model[, setdiff(names(costa_rica_model), "poor")])
Xd <- Xd[, apply(Xd, 2, sd) > 0]                      # drop constant columns
y  <- as.numeric(costa_rica_model$poor == "poor")
cors <- apply(Xd, 2, function(x) cor(x, y))

top <- head(cors[order(-abs(cors))], 12)
ggplot(data.frame(var = names(top), r = top), aes(reorder(var, abs(r)), r)) +
  geom_col() + coord_flip() + labs(x = NULL, y = "Correlation with poor")
```

The same information with one line per original variable (its strongest column):

```{r correlations-by-variable}
by_var <- split(cors, col_to_var(names(cors)))        # correlations grouped by variable
cor_tab <- data.frame(
  variable         = names(by_var),
  strongest_column = sapply(by_var, function(r) names(r)[which.max(abs(r))]),
  correlation      = sapply(by_var, function(r) r[which.max(abs(r))]),
  row.names = NULL)
cor_tab$type <- unname(var_type[cor_tab$variable])
cor_tab$correlation <- round(cor_tab$correlation, 3)
cor_tab <- cor_tab[order(-abs(cor_tab$correlation)),
                   c("variable", "type", "strongest_column", "correlation")]
knitr::kable(head(cor_tab, 15), row.names = FALSE,
             caption = "Strongest correlation with poverty for each variable")
```

These are simple associations that ignore all other variables.

# 6. Issues for the modelling stage

## 6.1 Rare categories (already handled in the cleaning step)

Some categories contain very few households. The effect of such a category cannot be
estimated reliably: with 22% poor households, a category of 30 households contains only about
7 poor ones. In the cleaning script we therefore removed every 0/1 column in which one of the
two values occurs in fewer than 30 households.

**No household was removed.** The households of a removed category stay in the data with 0 in
all remaining columns of that variable. Removing the households themselves would drop some
of the most deprived ones (for example no floor or no electricity), exactly the cases a
targeting programme most needs to find.

```{r category-counts}
cat_vars <- predictors[sapply(costa_rica[predictors], is.factor)]
counts <- do.call(rbind, lapply(cat_vars, function(v) {
  t <- table(costa_rica[[v]])
  data.frame(variable = v, category = names(t), n = as.integer(t),
             share_pct = round(100 * as.numeric(t) / nrow(costa_rica), 1))
}))
counts <- counts[order(counts$n), ]
rownames(counts) <- NULL
knitr::kable(head(counts, 15), caption = "The 15 rarest categories (readable data, before removal)")

knitr::kable(removed_cols, caption = "0/1 columns removed (fewer than 30 households)")
```

`r nrow(removed_cols)` columns were removed. The model data have
`r ncol(costa_rica_model) - 1` columns (predictors), all with at least 30 households in each
of their two values.

## 6.2 Strongly correlated columns

```{r issues}
cm <- cor(Xd)
h <- which(abs(cm) >= 0.9 & upper.tri(cm), arr.ind = TRUE)
high_pairs <- data.frame(var1 = rownames(cm)[h[, 1]], var2 = colnames(cm)[h[, 2]],
                         r = round(cm[h], 3))
high_pairs                                     # pairs with |correlation| >= 0.9
mean(costa_rica$monthly_rent > 0)              # share of households paying rent
```

`r nrow(high_pairs)` pairs of columns have an absolute correlation of at least 0.9 (mostly
categories of the same variable, and household size with persons living in the dwelling).
Regularization (lasso, ridge) handles this, and trees are not affected. Only
`r round(100 * mean(costa_rica$monthly_rent > 0), 1)`% of the households pay rent (for the
others the value is 0).

# 7. Main findings of the exploratory analysis

```{r key-numbers, echo=FALSE}
pr <- function(idx) 100 * mean(costa_rica$poor[idx] == "poor")   # poverty rate in %
r_edu_low  <- pr(which(edu_group == "none / incomplete primary"))
r_edu_high <- pr(which(edu_group == "higher"))
reg        <- tapply(costa_rica$poor == "poor", costa_rica$region, mean) * 100
r_central  <- reg["Central"]
r_other    <- range(reg[names(reg) != "Central"])
r_comp_yes <- pr(which(costa_rica$has_computer == 1))
r_comp_no  <- pr(which(costa_rica$has_computer == 0))
r_rural    <- pr(which(costa_rica$urban == 0))
r_urban    <- pr(which(costa_rica$urban == 1))
r_female   <- pr(which(costa_rica$head_male == 0))
r_male     <- pr(which(costa_rica$head_male == 1))
```

* **`r round(overall)`% of households are poor**: the classes are imbalanced, so accuracy
  alone is not informative.
* **Education is the strongest signal.** The poverty rate falls from
  `r round(r_edu_low)`% (head with no or incomplete primary education) to
  `r round(r_edu_high)`% (higher education). The variable with the strongest correlation to
  `poor` is `r cor_tab$variable[1]` (`r cor_tab$correlation[1]`).
* **Dwelling quality and assets matter.** Poverty is `r round(r_comp_yes)`% in households with
  a computer against `r round(r_comp_no)`% without. Households with bad floors or walls or no
  ceiling are also poorer (see the plots above).
* **Geography and sex of the head.** `r round(r_central)`% poor in the Central region against
  `r round(r_other[1])`-`r round(r_other[2])`% in the other regions; rural `r round(r_rural)`%
  against urban `r round(r_urban)`%; female-headed `r round(r_female)`% against male-headed
  `r round(r_male)`%.
* **No single variable is a strong predictor**: the largest absolute correlation is
  `r round(max(abs(cors)), 2)`. We need models that combine many variables.
* **Modelling implications.** The `r length(predictors)` predictors become
  `r ncol(Xd)` model columns when every category gets its own 0/1 column;
  `r nrow(high_pairs)` pairs of columns are strongly correlated. This motivates
  regularization (lasso) and variable selection inside cross-validation. Trees and boosting
  handle the skewed rent and the capped dependency rate without transformation.

**Sources.** Caruso, M., Galiani, S., Weinschelbaum, F. (2019). *Poverty Alleviation
Strategies Under Informality: Evidence for Latin America.* NBER Working Paper 26339.
Kim, J. Y. (2021). *Using Machine Learning to Predict Poverty Status in Costa Rican
Households.* arXiv:2111.13319. Data: Inter-American Development Bank via Kaggle.

# 8. Pre-processing and variable selection prior to the analysis

**Already done in the cleaning step** (it does not use the outcome, so there is no leakage):
one row per household; "yes"/"no" recoded; structural missing values set to 0; squared
copies, exact sums, duplicates and constant columns removed; one 0/1 column for every
category; 0/1 columns with fewer than 30 households removed.

**Steps before the models**

1. **Train/test split (70/30, stratified).** Following unit 4, we hold out a test set for the
   final assessment of the chosen model. The data set is not large, so tuning and model
   selection use 10-fold cross-validation on the training set instead of a separate validation
   set. The split is done first, with a fixed seed, and keeps the share of poor households in
   both parts. The test set is used only once, at the end.
2. **Encoding.** The model data already contain one 0/1 column per category, so all methods
   see exactly the same numeric matrix. Columns that are constant in the training set are
   removed.
3. **Scaling.** The penalty of the lasso depends on the scale of the variables, so they are
   standardized (`glmnet` does this internally and reports coefficients on the original
   scale). Trees and boosting are not affected by scale.
4. **Skewed variables (rent, dependency rate).** Left unchanged: tree-based methods are
   invariant to monotone transformations, and the penalty handles the rest.
5. **Class imbalance (22% poor).** We keep the natural class frequencies and evaluate with
   AUC, sensitivity and specificity instead of accuracy. The classification threshold can be
   adjusted afterwards (unit 4).
6. **Variable selection.** We do not drop variables by hand. Selecting variables by their
   relation to the outcome and then cross-validating would give an optimistic error (unit 4).
   Selection is part of the methods: the lasso sets coefficients exactly to zero, and for
   random forest and boosting we use variable importance. Everything is tuned by
   cross-validation on the training set only.

```{r preprocessing}
set.seed(2026)

# 1. stratified 70/30 split (same share of poor households in both parts)
idx_poor <- which(costa_rica$poor == "poor")
idx_not  <- which(costa_rica$poor == "not_poor")
train_id <- c(sample(idx_poor, round(0.7 * length(idx_poor))),
              sample(idx_not,  round(0.7 * length(idx_not))))
train <- costa_rica[train_id, ]      # same households, same order as costa_rica_model
test  <- costa_rica[-train_id, ]
table(train$poor); table(test$poor)
round(100 * prop.table(table(train$poor)), 1)
round(100 * prop.table(table(test$poor)), 1)

# 2. input matrices from the model data (one 0/1 column per category)
x_all   <- as.matrix(costa_rica_model[, setdiff(names(costa_rica_model), "poor")])
x_train <- x_all[train_id, ]
x_test  <- x_all[-train_id, ]
y_train <- train$poor
y_test  <- test$poor

# columns that are constant in the training set carry no information
keep <- apply(x_train, 2, sd) > 0
x_train <- x_train[, keep]
x_test  <- x_test[, keep]
dim(x_train)                         # training households x columns
```

# 9. Predictive models: lasso, random forest and boosting

We fit three methods from class to predict `poor`. All three use the same inputs (`x_train`,
`y_train`) and the same 10-fold cross-validation folds on the training set, so the comparison
is fair. The test set is not touched here.

| Method | Unit | Hyperparameters tuned by 10-fold CV |
|---|---|---|
| Logistic regression with lasso penalty (package glmnet) | 2-3 | penalty lambda |
| Random forest (package randomForest) | 6 | mtry (variables tried per split) |
| Boosting, gradient boosted trees (package gbm) | 7 | number of trees, tree depth, learning rate |

The tuning criterion is the AUC (area under the ROC curve), because the classes are
imbalanced and accuracy would be misleading.

## Step 1: Common set-up

A **hyperparameter** is a setting that the method does not learn from the data, and we have
to choose it. For each candidate value we fit on 9 folds, measure the AUC on the 10th fold, and
average over the 10 rounds. The folds are fixed once, so all methods are compared on exactly
the same folds. The folds run in parallel on several cores to save time.

The fitted models are saved in the folder `models`. If a saved model exists, it is loaded
instead of being fitted again. (Delete the folder `models` to refit everything, for example
after changing the data or the tuning grids.)

```{r cv-setup}
set.seed(2026)
folds <- createFolds(y_train, k = 10, returnTrain = TRUE)   # stratified folds

ctrl <- trainControl(
  method = "cv", number = 10, index = folds,   # same 10 folds for every method
  classProbs = TRUE,                           # probabilities are needed for the AUC
  summaryFunction = twoClassSummary)           # reports AUC ("ROC"), Sens, Spec
```

```{r helper-load-or-fit}
dir.create("models", showWarnings = FALSE)      # folder for the fitted models

# fits a model only if no saved file exists; otherwise loads the saved model
load_or_fit <- function(file, fit_expr) {
  path <- file.path("models", file)
  if (file.exists(path)) {
    message("Loading saved model: ", path)
    return(readRDS(path))
  }
  fit <- fit_expr                               # the model is fitted here, only when needed
  saveRDS(fit, path)
  fit
}
```

```{r parallel-start}
cl <- makePSOCKcluster(max(1, parallel::detectCores() - 1))   # all cores but one
registerDoParallel(cl)
```

## Step 2: Model 1 - Logistic regression with lasso penalty

The lasso fits a logistic regression and adds a penalty on the sum of the absolute values of
the coefficients. A larger lambda shrinks more, and weak variables get a coefficient of
exactly zero. A small lambda means little penalty (risk of overfitting); a large lambda
removes many variables (risk of underfitting). We try 30 values of lambda and keep the best one
by cross-validated AUC. (`alpha = 1` means lasso; the variables are standardized internally.)

```{r lasso}
set.seed(2026)
fit_lasso <- load_or_fit("fit_lasso.rds", train(
  x = x_train, y = y_train,
  method = "glmnet",
  metric = "ROC",                              # choose lambda by cross-validated AUC
  trControl = ctrl,
  tuneGrid = expand.grid(alpha = 1,            # alpha = 1: lasso
                         lambda = 10^seq(-4, -1, length.out = 30))))

fit_lasso$bestTune                             # chosen lambda
plot(fit_lasso)                                # CV-AUC for each lambda
```

How many columns does the lasso keep (coefficient not exactly zero)?

```{r lasso-kept}
cf_all <- as.matrix(coef(fit_lasso$finalModel, s = fit_lasso$bestTune$lambda))[-1, 1]
c(columns_total = length(cf_all), columns_kept = sum(cf_all != 0))
```

A positive coefficient raises the probability of being poor, a negative one lowers it,
holding the other variables fixed. The coefficients are discussed in section 12.

## Step 3: Model 2 - Random forest

A random forest grows many decision trees, each on a random bootstrap sample of the
households. At each split a tree may only look at a random subset of `mtry` variables. The
final prediction is the vote of all trees, which is much more stable than a single tree
(averaging reduces variance). We use 300 trees and tune `mtry`: a small `mtry` makes the
trees different from each other, a large `mtry` makes each tree stronger but more similar.

```{r random-forest}
set.seed(2026)
fit_rf <- load_or_fit("fit_rf.rds", train(
  x = x_train, y = y_train,
  method = "rf",
  metric = "ROC",
  trControl = ctrl,
  tuneGrid = data.frame(mtry = c(3, 6, 10, 15)),
  ntree = 300))

fit_rf$bestTune                                # chosen mtry
plot(fit_rf)                                   # CV-AUC for each mtry
```

Which variables matter most for the forest?

```{r rf-importance}
imp_rf <- varImp(fit_rf, scale = TRUE)$importance
imp_rf <- imp_rf[order(-imp_rf$Overall), , drop = FALSE]
knitr::kable(head(imp_rf, 15), digits = 1, caption = "Random forest: variable importance (100 = most important)")
```

## Step 4: Model 3 - Boosting

Boosting also uses trees, but builds them one after another: each small tree is fit to the
mistakes of the current model, and its contribution is added with a small weight (the learning
rate). Each step improves the model a little (boosting reduces bias). We tune three
hyperparameters:

* `n.trees`: number of trees (too many can overfit),
* `interaction.depth`: size of each tree (1 = single splits only, 3 = up to three variables
  interact),
* `shrinkage`: learning rate (small = slow, careful learning, needs more trees).

```{r boosting}
set.seed(2026)
fit_gbm <- load_or_fit("fit_gbm.rds", train(
  x = x_train, y = y_train,
  method = "gbm",
  metric = "ROC",
  trControl = ctrl,
  tuneGrid = expand.grid(n.trees = c(100, 300, 500),
                         interaction.depth = c(1, 2, 3),
                         shrinkage = c(0.01, 0.05),
                         n.minobsinnode = 10),   # minimum households per leaf (fixed)
  verbose = FALSE))

fit_gbm$bestTune                               # chosen combination
plot(fit_gbm)                                  # CV-AUC for each combination
```

```{r gbm-importance}
imp_gbm <- varImp(fit_gbm, scale = TRUE)$importance
imp_gbm <- imp_gbm[order(-imp_gbm$Overall), , drop = FALSE]
knitr::kable(head(imp_gbm, 15), digits = 1, caption = "Boosting: variable importance (100 = most important)")
```

```{r parallel-stop}
stopCluster(cl)                                # release the cores
registerDoSEQ()
```

## Step 5: Comparison of the three methods (cross-validation, training set)

Every method is shown with its best hyperparameters. The numbers are 10-fold CV estimates
computed on the same folds. The AUC ("ROC") is the main criterion. In this output "Sens" is the
share of not-poor households correctly found and "Spec" the share of poor households correctly
found, because caret treats the first factor level (not_poor) as the event. We therefore only
use the AUC here, and compute sensitivity and specificity of the poor class on the test set.

```{r comparison}
res <- resamples(list(Lasso = fit_lasso, RandomForest = fit_rf, Boosting = fit_gbm))
summary(res)
bwplot(res, metric = "ROC")                    # the 10 AUC values of each method
```

# 10. Model selection

We compare the three methods with the cross-validated AUC on the training set. All three
were evaluated on exactly the same 10 folds, so the comparison is fair and the test set plays
no role in the choice.

```{r selection}
cv_table <- data.frame(
  Method = c("Lasso", "Random forest", "Boosting"),
  Best_hyperparameters = c(
    paste0("lambda = ", signif(fit_lasso$bestTune$lambda, 3)),
    paste0("mtry = ", fit_rf$bestTune$mtry),
    paste0(fit_gbm$bestTune$n.trees, " trees, depth ",
           fit_gbm$bestTune$interaction.depth, ", learning rate ",
           fit_gbm$bestTune$shrinkage)),
  CV_AUC_mean = c(mean(res$values[["Lasso~ROC"]]),
                  mean(res$values[["RandomForest~ROC"]]),
                  mean(res$values[["Boosting~ROC"]])),
  CV_AUC_sd = c(sd(res$values[["Lasso~ROC"]]),
                sd(res$values[["RandomForest~ROC"]]),
                sd(res$values[["Boosting~ROC"]])))
cv_table[3:4] <- round(cv_table[3:4], 3)
knitr::kable(cv_table, row.names = FALSE, caption = "Cross-validated AUC on the training set")

# paired differences between methods over the 10 folds (t-tests, Bonferroni adjusted)
summary(diff(res, metric = "ROC"))
```

The cross-validated AUC is `r min(cv_table$CV_AUC_mean)` to `r max(cv_table$CV_AUC_mean)` for
the three methods, and the standard deviation across folds is about
`r round(mean(cv_table$CV_AUC_sd), 3)`. The differences between the methods are small compared
with this variation (see the paired tests), so we cannot say that one method predicts better
than the others. We therefore choose by **parsimony**: the **lasso** is the simplest model, it
is a linear model with coefficients that can be interpreted, and it predicts about as well as
the flexible tree ensembles. This also suggests that non-linear effects and interactions, which
the forest and boosting can capture, add little predictive power here.

**Check: ridge instead of lasso.** Ridge uses the same logistic regression with a penalty on
the sum of squared coefficients: it keeps all variables and shrinks correlated columns
together (unit 2). We tune it on the same folds to see whether it would be a better linear
model.

```{r ridge-check}
set.seed(2026)
fit_ridge <- load_or_fit("fit_ridge.rds", train(
  x = x_train, y = y_train,
  method = "glmnet", metric = "ROC", trControl = ctrl,
  tuneGrid = expand.grid(alpha = 0,                          # alpha = 0: ridge
                         lambda = 10^seq(-3, 1, length.out = 40))))

fit_ridge$bestTune                                           # should not be at the edge of the grid
res_lin <- resamples(list(Lasso = fit_lasso, Ridge = fit_ridge))
ridge_cmp <- data.frame(Method = c("Lasso", "Ridge"),
                        CV_AUC_mean = round(c(mean(res_lin$values[["Lasso~ROC"]]),
                                              mean(res_lin$values[["Ridge~ROC"]])), 3))
ridge_cmp
```

Ridge reaches a cross-validated AUC of `r ridge_cmp$CV_AUC_mean[2]`, against
`r ridge_cmp$CV_AUC_mean[1]` for the lasso. If the two are close, we keep the lasso, which
also selects variables.

# 11. Model assessment

The chosen model (lasso) is now assessed **once** on the test set, which was not used for
fitting or tuning. We report the AUC with the ROC curve, and the confusion matrix with
sensitivity and specificity of the poor class.

**Choice of the classification threshold.** The lasso outputs a probability of being poor. The
default rule "poor if probability >= 0.5" is a poor fit for imbalanced data: with only 22%
poor households the model tends to say "not poor". We therefore also use a second threshold
that maximizes sensitivity + specificity (Youden index). To avoid using the test set for this
choice, it is computed on out-of-fold predictions of the training set: each training household
is predicted by a lasso (with the chosen lambda) that was fit on the other folds.

```{r threshold}
best_lambda <- fit_lasso$bestTune$lambda
oof <- rep(NA_real_, nrow(x_train))
for (f in folds) {                                  # f = rows used for fitting in this fold
  hold  <- setdiff(seq_len(nrow(x_train)), f)       # rows held out in this fold
  fit_f <- glmnet(x_train[f, ], y_train[f], family = "binomial",
                  alpha = 1, lambda = best_lambda)
  oof[hold] <- as.numeric(predict(fit_f, newx = x_train[hold, ], type = "response"))
}

roc_oof <- roc(y_train, oof, levels = c("not_poor", "poor"), direction = "<", quiet = TRUE)
thr <- as.numeric(coords(roc_oof, x = "best", best.method = "youden",
                         ret = "threshold", transpose = FALSE)[1, "threshold"])
c(cv_AUC = as.numeric(auc(roc_oof)), chosen_threshold = thr)
```

```{r assessment}
# predicted probability of being poor for the test households
p_test   <- predict(fit_lasso, newdata = x_test, type = "prob")[, "poor"]
roc_test <- roc(y_test, p_test, levels = c("not_poor", "poor"), direction = "<", quiet = TRUE)
auc_test <- as.numeric(auc(roc_test))
auc_ci   <- as.numeric(ci.auc(roc_test))            # 95% confidence interval
c(AUC = auc_test, lower = auc_ci[1], upper = auc_ci[3])

plot(roc_test, legacy.axes = TRUE, print.auc = TRUE,
     main = "ROC curve of the lasso on the test set")

# confusion matrix and measures for a given threshold
assess <- function(prob, truth, cutoff) {
  pred <- factor(ifelse(prob >= cutoff, "poor", "not_poor"), levels = c("not_poor", "poor"))
  cm <- confusionMatrix(pred, truth, positive = "poor")
  print(cm$table)
  data.frame(Threshold   = round(cutoff, 3),
             Accuracy    = round(unname(cm$overall["Accuracy"]), 3),
             Sensitivity = round(unname(cm$byClass["Sensitivity"]), 3),   # poor households found
             Specificity = round(unname(cm$byClass["Specificity"]), 3),   # not-poor households found
             Precision   = round(unname(cm$byClass["Pos Pred Value"]), 3))
}
cat("Threshold 0.5\n");  r1 <- assess(p_test, y_test, 0.5)
cat("\nThreshold chosen on the training set\n"); r2 <- assess(p_test, y_test, thr)
res_tab <- rbind(r1, r2)
knitr::kable(res_tab, row.names = FALSE, caption = "Test set: lasso at two thresholds")

# benchmark: accuracy of the rule "nobody is poor"
bench <- round(mean(y_test == "not_poor"), 3)
bench
```

```{r test-auc-all}
# for information only: test AUC of all three methods (not used for the selection)
test_auc <- sapply(list(Lasso = fit_lasso, RandomForest = fit_rf, Boosting = fit_gbm),
  function(m) {
    p <- predict(m, newdata = x_test, type = "prob")[, "poor"]
    as.numeric(auc(roc(y_test, p, levels = c("not_poor", "poor"), direction = "<", quiet = TRUE)))
  })
round(test_auc, 3)
```

**Results.** On the test set the lasso has an AUC of `r round(auc_test, 3)` (95% interval
`r round(auc_ci[1], 3)` to `r round(auc_ci[3], 3)`), to be compared with the cross-validated
`r cv_table$CV_AUC_mean[1]`. Similar values mean that the model generalizes and there is no
sign of overfitting. The AUC is the probability that a randomly chosen poor household gets a
higher score than a randomly chosen non-poor one.

With the default threshold of 0.5 the model finds `r round(100 * res_tab$Sensitivity[1], 1)`%
of the poor households (sensitivity) and `r round(100 * res_tab$Specificity[1], 1)`% of the
non-poor ones (specificity). Its accuracy is `r round(100 * res_tab$Accuracy[1], 1)`%, to be
compared with `r round(100 * bench, 1)`% for the rule "nobody is poor": accuracy alone says
little here. With the threshold `r round(thr, 2)` chosen on the training set, sensitivity
becomes `r round(100 * res_tab$Sensitivity[2], 1)`% and specificity
`r round(100 * res_tab$Specificity[2], 1)`%: the model finds more poor households, at the
price of wrongly flagging more non-poor ones (precision
`r round(100 * res_tab$Precision[2], 1)`%). Which threshold is right is a **policy decision**,
because wrongly excluding a poor household and wrongly including a non-poor one have different
costs.

# 12. Insights on the final model

**Which characteristics are associated with poverty?** Every category has its own 0/1 column,
and numeric variables enter as they are. A positive coefficient raises the probability of
being poor, a negative one lowers it, holding the other variables fixed (the unit is the
log-odds). Coefficients of different types of variables are not comparable in size: a numeric
coefficient is the effect of one unit, a category coefficient is the effect of belonging to
that category. We therefore also show the **effect per standard deviation** (the coefficient
times the standard deviation of its column): it measures the effect of a typical difference
and is automatically small for rare categories.

```{r insights-lasso}
cf <- as.matrix(coef(fit_lasso$finalModel, s = best_lambda))[-1, 1]   # drop the intercept
cf <- cf[cf != 0]                                                      # columns kept
col_var <- col_to_var(names(cf))
eff <- data.frame(variable      = col_var,
                  type          = unname(var_type[col_var]),
                  column        = names(cf),
                  coefficient   = unname(cf),
                  effect_per_sd = unname(cf * apply(x_train[, names(cf), drop = FALSE], 2, sd)))
eff$direction <- ifelse(eff$coefficient > 0, "more poor", "less poor")
eff <- eff[order(-abs(eff$effect_per_sd)), ]
rownames(eff) <- NULL
nrow(eff)                                                              # columns kept by the lasso

eff_show <- data.frame(
  column        = eff$column,
  coefficient   = formatC(eff$coefficient, format = "fg", digits = 3),   # no scientific notation
  effect_per_sd = round(eff$effect_per_sd, 3))
knitr::kable(head(eff_show, 15), row.names = FALSE, align = "lrr",
             caption = "Lasso: the 15 largest effects per standard deviation (positive = more poor)")

ggplot(head(eff, 15), aes(reorder(column, abs(effect_per_sd)), effect_per_sd, fill = direction)) +
  geom_col() + coord_flip() +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Effect per standard deviation (log-odds)", fill = NULL)
```

The two tree-based models give a second view that does not depend on the linear form (the
importance tables above). Their top-10 rankings:

```{r importance-compare}
top_rf  <- rownames(head(imp_rf, 10))
top_gbm <- rownames(head(imp_gbm, 10))
knitr::kable(data.frame(rank = 1:10, random_forest = top_rf, boosting = top_gbm))
common <- intersect(top_rf, top_gbm)
common                                          # variables in both top-10 lists
```

**What the model tells us**

* The three largest lasso effects are `r paste(head(eff$column, 3), collapse = ", ")`. The
  variables in the top 10 of both the random forest and boosting are
  `r if (length(common) > 0) paste(common, collapse = ", ") else "none"`. Variables that
  appear in several rankings are the most reliable signals.
* The exploratory analysis pointed to education, household composition, crowding and dwelling
  quality. Check in the tables above that the same groups of variables appear at the top; this
  is what the logic of a proxy means test would suggest.
* The lasso predicts about as well as the forest and boosting (test AUC: lasso
  `r round(test_auc["Lasso"], 3)`, random forest `r round(test_auc["RandomForest"], 3)`,
  boosting `r round(test_auc["Boosting"], 3)`). The relationship between the characteristics
  and poverty is therefore mostly additive and roughly linear on the log-odds scale.

**Limits of the model**

* The results are **associations, not causal effects**: giving a household a computer would not
  necessarily lift it out of poverty.
* Coefficients are conditional on all other variables, and correlated variables can take
  unexpected signs. For example `overcrowded_rooms` and `overcrowded_bedrooms` can get a
  negative coefficient, although crowded households are poorer on their own, because
  `persons_per_bedroom` already contains most of this information.
* An AUC of about `r round(auc_test, 2)` is a moderate discrimination: the characteristics
  predict poverty clearly better than chance (0.5), but a sizeable share of poor households
  look like non-poor ones. This is the known limit of proxy means tests under informality.
* The data describe the household head and the dwelling and come from one survey. The classes
  are imbalanced, so the choice of the threshold matters as much as the choice of the method.
* The test performance is estimated on one random split. A different split would give a
  slightly different number; the cross-validated AUC and its spread show how much.
